name: Freya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Freya, thanks for doing this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, of course. I lead a crew of five on the coast, working out of the depot in Port Avel, and we cover everything from the overhead lines along the cliff road to the underground cable in the old town. Salt is our enemy, it eats the fittings, so a lot of my week is replacing corroded clamps and chasing faults after storms. I also fly the depot's inspection drone, which I fought for two years to get.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving the puzzle when a feeder trips and nobody knows why. I'll have the outage map up on my phone, ask an AI assistant to sort the customer calls by street, and usually I can guess the fault before we roll out. What wears me out is the pay, which is low because we're a small coastal depot, and the fact that there's nowhere else to go around here unless I want to drive three hours a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use an AI assistant. How much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to draft switching plans, which I then check against the network diagram, to translate manuals for the new recloser units, and to write the boring emails to head office. My partner Jo teases me that I talk to it more than to him, which isn't true, but it's close some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a waste of all that hype, but I'd still keep using the tools, because they're handy. On the crew chat I'd post something like at least the drone still works. Some of the older guys would be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I like new stuff, and I'd hoped AI would take the paperwork off us so we could do more real work. But for my pay and my job, it'd be fine, just the same grind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal and keep using the tools I already use. I'd push the union to use any time we save on paperwork to argue for an extra person on each crew, because we're stretched. And I'd keep trying to save, which right now means about forty a month, if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like a party that never got started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is saving so hard for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the low pay, and partly because I lent my sister two months of rent when she left a bad relationship, and she's paying it back slowly. I don't regret it. But it means if my car fails its safety test, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your crew say if the AI hype fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, who's been on the job thirty years, would say I told you, girl, and I'd let him have it. Then he'd ask me to sort out his timesheet on my phone like he does every week.

S0.say: I'd say what a waste of all that hype, but I'd keep using the tools because they're handy. On the crew chat I'd post that at least the drone still works.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped AI would take the paperwork off us so we could do more real work. For my job and pay, it'd be the same grind.
S0.do: Carries on using the AI tools she already uses and pushes the union to turn saved paperwork time into an extra person per crew. Keeps saving about forty a month while her sister pays back a loan.
S0.feel: Calm but a little flat, like a party that never got started.
S0.quote: Then he'd ask me to sort out his timesheet on my phone like he does every week.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is the depot's early adopter and finds a fizzle slightly disappointing rather than reassuring. Her savings are thin partly from low pay and partly from lending her sister rent money. Her progressive streak shows in wanting saved time to fund more staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, but bring the workers with it. Online I'd probably post about how drones have already cut our patrol time in half and nobody lost a job, because we did more repairs instead. I'd want that to be the model everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'm the one already using this stuff, so I'd likely end up running the drone fleet or training others. The bit I'd worry about is whether head office uses it to cut crews instead of adding work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer straight away to pilot any new tool at our depot, before head office picks someone who's never been up a pole. I'd sign up for the advanced drone licence, which costs about four hundred, and ask the union to make the company pay for it. I'd also start writing up how we use AI at Port Avel, so there's a worker's version on file when they make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly. This is the version where I get to shape things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do well. Is there anyone at the depot you think wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, for sure. He's the best rigger I know, but he still prints out emails. I'd want to make sure he's paired with me or someone who'll do the screen side while he does what he's brilliant at, otherwise they'll push him out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the four hundred for the licence come from if the company says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay it in instalments, and I'd skip the weekend trip Jo and I planned for my birthday. He'd understand. He fixes bikes, he knows what it's like to buy your own tools.

S1.say: Bring it on, but bring the workers with it. I'd post that drones already halved our patrol time and nobody lost a job, because we did more repairs instead.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, since I'm already using this stuff and would likely run the drone fleet or train others. I'd worry about head office using it to cut crews instead of adding work.
S1.do: Volunteers to pilot any new tool at her depot and signs up for a four-hundred advanced drone licence, asking the union to get the company to pay. Writes up how her crew uses AI so a worker's view is on file.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, because she'd get to shape things.
S1.quote: I'd volunteer straight away to pilot any new tool at our depot, before head office picks someone who's never been up a pole.
S1.fieldNote: She'd move first, but always with an eye on her crew, especially the older rigger Mick. She'd pay for her own licence if needed, even at the cost of a birthday trip. Her worry is about management choices, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the grid should be publicly run if machines are going to do the work, because otherwise all the savings go to shareholders while whole towns like Port Avel lose their wages. I'd be on the union's online campaigns every day. I'd also say the people who know the network should be running the robots, not some contractor from the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is tight even for me. I'd have the skills to move, but I'd have no money to move with, and the jobs that open up would probably be in the cities, at the robot companies' control centres. I'd be one of the lucky ones who could jump, but jumping costs money I haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask head office for a role supervising the robot crews and put it in writing. I'd cut everything, no takeaways, sell my old motorbike, and get my sister to pay back what she can. If the only real jobs were in the city, I'd talk to Jo about moving within the year, even though it'd break my heart to leave the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel like I could handle it, but it'd be a sprint with no water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leaving the coast mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything I like about my life is here, the sea, Jo's bike shop, my mum twenty minutes away. If I left, Jo would have to start again too, and his shop is his whole thing. That's the conversation I'd dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose with only two years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to build something here. With more time, I could push for a local robot crew run out of Port Avel. With two years, it's whoever gets there first, and that's not going to be a small depot on the coast.

S2.say: If machines are going to do the work, the grid should be publicly run, or the savings all go to shareholders while towns like Port Avel lose their wages. People who know the network should run the robots.
S2.think: Two years is tight even for me, because I'd have the skills to move but no money to move with. The new jobs would probably be in city control centres, and jumping costs money I haven't got.
S2.do: Asks head office in writing for a role supervising robot crews within the first month. Cuts spending, sells her motorbike, calls in her sister's loan and discusses moving to the city with her partner within the year.
S2.feel: Anxious but capable, like a sprint with no water.
S2.quote: I'd be one of the lucky ones who could jump, but jumping costs money I haven't got.
S2.fieldNote: Even for the most adaptable person in the depot, thin savings turn a fast change into real pressure. Her skills give her options, but most of those options are far from the coast and her partner's business. She frames the issue as who owns the savings from automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up worker-run robot crews at every depot, if the company and government want it. I'd be making that case at union meetings and online. I'd be the annoying one with the slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one feels much better. Five years is enough to get qualified on the robot side, save a bit and push for the work to stay here. I'd probably be fine, and I could help others get through too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start the robotics technician course part-time, there's one at the technical college an hour away. I'd push head office to make Port Avel the trial depot for robot crews, with our people operating them. I'd save every bit of overtime, aiming for two months of savings by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mostly hopeful way. There's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the annoying one with the slides. Who would you be trying to convince?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The regional manager, Helen. She's not a bad person, she just thinks in budgets. If I can show her a worker-run trial saves money and keeps the depot open, she'd go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years rather than two change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to leave the coast. With two years I'd be chasing jobs in the city. With five I can try to bring the new jobs here.

S3.say: Five years is enough to set up worker-run robot crews at every depot, if the company and government want it. I'd be the annoying one with the slides at union meetings.
S3.think: This one feels much better, because five years is enough to qualify on the robot side, save a bit and keep the work here. I'd probably be fine and could help others through.
S3.do: Starts a part-time robotics technician course at a college an hour away in year one. Pushes head office to make her depot the trial site for worker-operated robot crews, and saves overtime to reach two months of savings by year two.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, because there's a plan.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be chasing jobs in the city. With five I can try to bring the new jobs here.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years shift her from leaving to building locally. She has a specific target in the regional manager, Helen, and a concrete pitch based on budgets. Her idea of a worker-run trial mixes progressive values with real enthusiasm for the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best-case version, so let's not waste it. Ten years is enough to retrain everyone who wants it and to put proper public control on the new systems. I'd post that the grid should belong to the people who use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd thrive. I'd be thirty-seven, running robot crews for the coast, and maybe teaching apprentices how to work alongside them. I'd still have thin savings, probably, but my skills would be worth a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd keep using the tools, get the drone and robotics qualifications over the next few years, and push for Port Avel to trial every new system early. I'd stand for the union's regional committee so I can help write the transition rules. And I'd vote and campaign for public ownership of the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. This feels like a future I'd want to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my friends outside the trade might not land as softly. Jo's bike shop could be fine, but my mate Laila does data entry, and ten years doesn't help her if nobody gives her a path. I'd want that sorted, not just my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything in your personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I want kids at some point, and this version makes me feel braver about it. With two years I'd be putting that off. With ten I'd think, all right, we can probably do this.

S4.say: This is the best-case version, so let's not waste it. Ten years is enough to retrain everyone who wants it and put public control on the new systems.
S4.think: I think I'd thrive, running robot crews for the coast at thirty-seven and maybe teaching apprentices to work alongside them. My savings might still be thin, but my skills would be worth a lot more.
S4.do: Keeps using AI tools, gets drone and robotics qualifications over the next few years and pushes for her depot to trial new systems early. Stands for the union's regional committee and campaigns for public ownership of the grid.
S4.feel: Calm, even hopeful, as if this is a future she'd want to live in.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be putting that off. With ten I'd think, all right, we can probably do this.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's openly optimistic and even feels braver about having children. Her concern moves outward to friends like Laila who lack a path. Her politics and her love of new tools sit together comfortably here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have the skills but not the money, and the jobs would be far from here. What would help is money to retrain and relocate, and a rule that local depots get first shot at running the new robot crews, so towns like Port Avel don't just empty out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to decide. Everyone talks about whether robots can do the work, but the real question is who owns them. If the people who climb the poles help run the robots, I'm all for it.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about whether robots can do the work, but the real question is who owns them.
portrait: Freya Garcia is a 27-year-old crew leader at a small coastal depot, the person who fought to get an inspection drone and uses AI tools every day. She's low paid and has little saved, partly because she lent her sister rent money. She stays calm and even excited through the slow scenarios, gets anxious with AGI in two years because she has skills but no money to move, and grows hopeful with more time. Throughout, she wants workers and the public to own and run the new machines, and she'd rather bring the new jobs to Port Avel than leave.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have the skills but not the money, and the new jobs would be far from the coast.
whatWouldHelp: Money to retrain and relocate, and a rule that local depots get first shot at running the new robot crews.
